readerTitle: The sentence that made children avoid hard problems
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Mueller & Dweck 1998 칭찬 실험, Heslin 외 2005 관리자 평가 연구, Sisk 외 2018 메타분석) + 가상 적용 (사내 재무팀, 원예용품 소매점)
insight: 실패를 '나는 어떤 사람인가'에 대한 판정이 아니라 '다음에 무엇을 바꿀까'에 대한 정보로 읽으면 어려운 일을 피하지 않게 된다.
misconception: 성장 마인드셋은 긍정적으로 생각하고 더 열심히 노력하는 것이다. 또는 마음가짐만 바꾸면 성과가 크게 오른다.

sources.text: Mueller, C. M., & Dweck, C. S. (1998). Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75(1), 33–52.
Dweck, C. S. (2006). Mindset: The New Psychology of Success. Random House.
Heslin, P. A., Latham, G. P., & VandeWalle, D. (2005). The effect of implicit person theory on performance appraisals. Journal of Applied Psychology, 90(5), 842–856.
Sisk, V. F., et al. (2018). To what extent and under which circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? Two meta-analyses. Psychological Science, 29(4), 549–571.
Yeager, D. S., et al. (2019). A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement. Nature, 573, 364–369.
Dweck, C. S. (2015). Carol Dweck revisits the 'growth mindset'. Education Week.

factChecks.note: Mueller & Dweck(1998)의 세부 결과(지능 칭찬 집단이 쉬운 과제를 더 많이 고름, 어려운 문제 후 즐거움·성과 하락, 점수를 부풀려 말한 비율이 더 높음)를 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적 비율 없이 방향만 적었습니다. 대상이 5학년(약 10~11세)인지도 확인 필요.
Heslin 외(2005): 고정 관점을 가진 관리자가 직원의 성과 향상을 덜 알아차리고 첫인상에 고정되는 경향이 있다는 결과인지 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 일반적으로만 서술했습니다.
Sisk 외(2018) 메타분석의 '효과가 전반적으로 약함', Yeager 외(2019)의 '성적이 낮은 학생에게서 작지만 의미 있는 효과' 요약이 정확한지 확인하세요.
'false growth mindset'(노력만 칭찬하는 오용)에 대한 Dweck의 경고는 2015년 Education Week 기고 기준입니다. 표현을 게시 전 확인하세요.

cards.title: The sentence that made children avoid hard problems
body: Two groups of children solve the same puzzles and get the same good score. The only difference is one sentence of praise afterward.
A few minutes later, the two groups start making very different choices about what to try next.

image.label: Two children at desks with identical puzzle sheets, one speech bubble above each
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 두 아이가 똑같은 퍼즐 종이를 들고 있고, 각자 위에 말풍선 하나. 왼쪽 "You must be smart", 오른쪽 "You must have worked hard". 배경은 단순한 교실. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your first big presentation went badly.
body: You lead a new forecasting project inside your company's finance team. Your first update to senior leadership went poorly: you lost the room on the numbers and ran out of time.
Your boss asks if you want to keep presenting next quarter. What do you do?

options.text: Hand it to a colleague who is a natural presenter
options.feedback: The next meeting may go smoother. But you've decided presenting is a fixed trait you lack, and you lose the practice you'd need to ever get better.

options.text: Keep it, ask two attendees what lost them, and rehearse with a colleague
options.feedback: You treat the bad meeting as information about what to change. It costs time and some discomfort, and it builds a skill you'll need again.

options.text: Keep it and spend more evenings polishing the slides alone
options.feedback: Good that you're not giving up. But more effort on the same approach, without knowing what went wrong, may just produce a prettier version of the same meeting.

cards.title: Praise for being smart made children play it safe.
body: In studies published in 1998, psychologists Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck gave fifth graders a set of puzzles. Afterward, some heard "You must be smart at this." Others heard "You must have worked hard."
Then the children picked their next task: one where they could learn something new, or one where they would look good. Children praised for being smart more often chose the safe one.
After a harder round, they also enjoyed the puzzles less, did worse on a later set, and were more likely to overstate their scores.

cards.title: Growth mindset
body: A **growth mindset** is the belief that your abilities can be developed through practice, good strategies and help from others. A *fixed mindset* treats abilities as something you either have or don't.
The difference shows up after a setback. With a fixed mindset, failure is a verdict on who you are, so you avoid risky tasks. With a growth mindset, failure is information about what to change next.

image.label: Same stumble, two readings: a verdict stamp vs a notebook of next steps
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 넘어진 막대 그래프 하나(실패). 왼쪽 화살표는 "Verdict: I'm not good at this" 도장, 오른쪽 화살표는 "Data: what to change next" 메모장. 오른쪽을 밝은 색으로 강조.

cards.title: Listen to how you explain a setback.
body: Mindset is less a mood than a habit of explanation. You can hear it in the sentences you use after something goes wrong.
list: "I'm not a numbers person" → "I haven't learned this *yet*"
"They're just better at this" → "What are they doing that I'm not?"
"That was a disaster" → "Which part broke, and what would fix it?"
cards.callout: The second version always points to a next step you can take.
cards.softwareNote: Many software teams run *blameless postmortems* after an outage. The failure is treated as information about the system, not a verdict on the engineer, so people report problems instead of hiding them.

cards.title: Your mindset shapes how you judge your team.
body: The same beliefs show up when you manage people. In a 2005 study, Peter Heslin and colleagues found that managers who believed people's abilities were mostly fixed tended to stick with their first impressions. They were slower to notice when an employee improved.
So a fixed view of others has a hidden cost. You stop investing in people who could grow, and you miss it when they do.

cards.title: It's not just effort, and it's not magic.
body: Effort alone isn't a growth mindset. Dweck has warned against praising effort that isn't working. Growth needs new strategies and feedback, not just more hours.

And the effects are smaller than popular books suggest. A 2018 review of many studies found weak effects of mindset training overall. A large 2019 study found small but real gains, mostly for students who were struggling.
Mindset helps you keep learning. It doesn't replace skill, time or support.

cards.title: Now it's a garden-supply store.
body: You own three garden-supply stores. Your business partner always did the seasonal buying, but she has left. Your first spring order went badly: too many tools, not enough seedlings.
What do you do before the next season?

options.text: Hire an experienced buyer. You just don't have the eye for it
options.feedback: Hiring may be the right business call. But if the reason is "I'm not a buyer", you skip learning a skill that drives most of your profit.

options.text: Compare what sold to what you ordered, ask suppliers and your ex-partner for advice, and test smaller orders
options.feedback: You turn one bad season into specific lessons and limit the cost of new mistakes. It's slower than hiring, but you build judgment you'll keep.

options.text: Order the same way next season, just more carefully
options.feedback: It feels like persistence. Without finding out what went wrong, extra care is unlikely to fix it.

cards.softwareNote: The same move works in a software business: compare what users actually did after a launch with what you expected, then run a small test before the next big release.

cards.title: Read a setback as information, not a verdict.
body: What you tell yourself after failing decides whether you try again, and whether you try differently.
**Try it today:** finish the sentence "I'm not a ___ person." Add the word *yet*, then name one specific way to practice it this week, and one person who could give you feedback.
